title: Trump Calls Ballroom Lawsuit Opponents “Treasonists” as Court Halts Work
description_medium: On August 14, 2026, Donald Trump attacked the National Trust for Historic Preservation on Truth Social after a federal appeals court upheld an order halting above-ground construction on his planned White House ballroom unless Congress authorizes it. Trump accused the preservation group of exposing military secrets and called its members “treasonists.” The court allowed national-security work, including an underground facility, to continue; the Trust says it supports necessary security construction.
description_long: President Donald Trump’s plan to build a ballroom on the site of the demolished White House East Wing faced another setback in August 2026, when a federal appeals court upheld an injunction pausing above-ground construction unless Congress approves the project. The National Trust for Historic Preservation had sued to stop the work, arguing that major changes to the White House required congressional authorization. The court distinguished the proposed ballroom from national-security work and allowed an underground facility to continue. On August 14, Trump responded on Truth Social by calling the Trust’s members “treasonists” and claiming that the lawsuit disclosed top-secret military features of the project. The Independent reported that Trump said military officials had warned the group not to sue, while public plans for a rooftop drone facility had already been discussed by the president. Trump and the Justice Department argued that the ballroom and associated security construction were important to protect the president and visitors; the Trust said it was not challenging necessary security work. The episode joined a legal dispute over presidential authority to alter federal property with a political fight over the project’s purpose, cost, and claimed security needs. At the time, above-ground construction was paused while Trump sought further review, and the court had not accepted his accusation that the lawsuit exposed secrets as proof of wrongdoing by the Trust.

corrected_wording.original_claim: The National Trust for Historic Preservation launched a lawsuit to stop Trump’s ballroom after revealing top military secrets.
corrected_wording.corrected: The Trust sued to halt construction; Trump accused it of disclosing secrets, but the cited coverage presents that as his claim, not an established finding.

source_access_notes: Opened The Independent report and used its same-event account of the appeals court order and Trump’s Truth Social post.
rationale: Expanded the item from a social-media outburst to the court ruling that prompted it and attributed Trump’s national-security and treason allegations.

title: Democrats Criticize Trump’s Washington Construction Projects at Shadow Hearing
description_medium: On July 21, 2026, congressional Democrats held an unofficial “shadow hearing” on President Trump’s construction projects in Washington, including the White House ballroom and a planned triumphal arch. Witnesses and lawmakers criticized the projects as vanity efforts and raised concerns about no-bid contracts, donors, and potential conflicts of interest. Republicans did not participate, so the forum was not official congressional business, and no court had found that the administration violated contracting laws.
description_long: House and Senate Democrats held an unofficial shadow hearing on July 21, 2026, to examine President Donald Trump’s construction and renovation projects around Washington. Lawmakers focused on the East Wing demolition and proposed White House ballroom, the renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, and a planned triumphal arch. They criticized the projects as “vanity” efforts and raised questions about expedited no-bid contracts and potential conflicts between donors to privately financed projects and administration actions. CBS News reported that one contract went to a water-filtration company owned by a Trump political donor and neighbor. Witnesses included former Obama White House ethics lawyer Norm Eisen, Public Citizen lawyer Jon Golinger, musician Ben Folds, and D.C. Delegate Eleanor Holmes Norton. Democrats also discussed the Kennedy Center, where artists had canceled shows and the board had announced a two-year closure for renovations after Trump became chairman. Republicans did not participate, and the lawmakers sat at temporary tables rather than the raised dais used for formal proceedings; the event was therefore political oversight activity, not an official committee hearing. Some Democrats said they lacked subpoena power while out of the majority and promised investigations if they regained control. The coverage reported allegations and questions raised at the forum, while noting that no court had found the administration violated government contracting laws.

corrected_wording.original_claim: The projects demonstrate disregard for norms and potential conflicts of interest.
corrected_wording.corrected: Democratic lawmakers and witnesses criticized the projects and raised potential conflict-of-interest concerns at an unofficial hearing; the concerns were not adjudicated findings.

source_access_notes: Used CBS News coverage of the July 21, 2026 shadow hearing, including the projects, witnesses, and procedural status.
rationale: Replaced a generic summary with the hearing date, named projects and witnesses, and clarified that it was unofficial and raised concerns rather than issuing findings.

title: BBC Seeks Court Approval to Subpoena Trump Family in Defamation Case
description_medium: The BBC asked a federal court in Florida to authorize subpoenas seeking testimony and records from Donald Trump Jr., Ivanka Trump, and Jared Kushner as it defended against Trump’s $10 billion defamation lawsuit. The case concerns a 2024 BBC documentary that edited his January 6, 2021 speech. The BBC argued the relatives had relevant knowledge of Trump’s actions that day; his lawyers called the request harassment. The request was for court permission, not a ruling that the relatives must testify.
description_long: In August 2026, the BBC asked a federal court in Florida for permission to subpoena Donald Trump Jr., Ivanka Trump, and Jared Kushner for testimony and documents in President Donald Trump’s $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the broadcaster. Trump sued over a 2024 BBC Panorama documentary that edited portions of his January 6, 2021 speech before the Capitol attack. His lawyers allege that the program spliced two excerpts, recorded about 55 minutes apart, in a way that falsely suggested he explicitly called for violence; the BBC apologized for the edit but argues it does not support a defamation claim. The broadcaster said the three relatives may have firsthand knowledge relevant to Trump’s account of his actions and intentions that day. The BBC’s filing cited congressional records showing Donald Trump Jr. and Ivanka Trump were present in the Oval Office while Trump revised his speech, and that Kushner drafted a statement condemning the violence. The BBC had previously tried to serve the relatives but reported difficulty reaching them, including at their Florida home and Trump Tower. Trump’s legal team accused the network of abusing the deposition process and asked the court to reject the request. The filing sought authorization to serve third-party subpoenas; it did not itself compel testimony or establish the merits of either side’s defamation arguments.

corrected_wording.original_claim: The BBC is attempting to force Donald Trump’s family to testify in a £7 billion lawsuit related to allegations made by the Trump family against the BBC.
corrected_wording.corrected: The BBC asked a Florida court to authorize third-party subpoenas for Donald Trump Jr., Ivanka Trump, and Jared Kushner in Donald Trump’s $10 billion defamation suit over a 2024 Panorama edit of his January 6 speech.

source_access_notes: The supplied Daily Mail URL was not opened. Used same-event CBS News and AP reporting; clarified that the BBC sought court authorization and that Trump is the plaintiff.
rationale: Corrected the direction of the lawsuit and the procedural description: the BBC sought permission to subpoena relatives in Trump’s pending suit.

title: BBC Seeks Subpoenas for Trump Relatives in January 6 Speech Lawsuit
description_medium: The BBC asked a Florida federal court to authorize subpoenas for Donald Trump Jr., Ivanka Trump, and Jared Kushner in its defense against President Donald Trump’s $10 billion defamation suit. The case concerns a 2024 Panorama edit of Trump’s January 6, 2021 speech. The BBC said the relatives may have relevant firsthand information; Trump’s lawyers called the request an abuse of the deposition process. At this stage the request sought permission to serve subpoenas, not a court order compelling testimony.
description_long: The BBC sought help from a federal court in Florida in August 2026 to obtain testimony and documents from Donald Trump Jr., Ivanka Trump, and Jared Kushner. The request arose in President Donald Trump’s $10 billion defamation lawsuit over a 2024 Panorama documentary that edited his January 6, 2021 speech. Trump alleges the BBC spliced two portions of the speech, delivered about 55 minutes apart, to make it seem he directly called for violence at the Capitol. The BBC apologized for the edit but maintains that the program does not amount to defamation. In its filing, the broadcaster argued the relatives had personal knowledge relevant to Trump’s claims: congressional records show Donald Trump Jr. and Ivanka Trump were present while Trump revised his speech, and Kushner drafted a statement condemning the violence after the attack began. The BBC said earlier attempts to serve subpoenas had failed, including attempts at the family’s Florida home and Trump Tower. Trump’s lawyers opposed the request, saying it would harass his family and supporters. The BBC asked the court to authorize service of third-party subpoenas; the filing was a discovery request, not a decision requiring the relatives to testify. The underlying lawsuit and disputes over the edit and its effect on viewers remained unresolved.

corrected_wording.original_claim: The BBC is seeking to compel Trump’s family to testify in a defamation lawsuit worth £7 billion brought by the Trump family.
corrected_wording.corrected: The BBC asked to subpoena three Trump relatives in Donald Trump’s $10 billion defamation suit against the broadcaster; the court request concerned discovery and had not yet compelled testimony.

source_access_notes: The supplied Daily Mail page was not opened; CBS and AP reports cover the same court filing and clarify who sued whom and what relief the BBC requested.
rationale: Corrected the duplicated entry’s misleading account of parties, amount, and procedural status while retaining the significant request and its relevance to the January 6 speech.

title: Chicago Prosecutors Subpoena Democratic Consulting Firm Linked to Judge’s Daughter
description_medium: A Chicago federal investigation subpoenaed records from Authentic Campaigns, a Democratic political consulting firm once co-owned by Loren Merchan, daughter of New York judge Juan Merchan, who presided over Donald Trump’s hush-money trial. The Emptywheel post says prosecutor Matthew Skiba helped secure the subpoena with colleague William Hogan. It links this investigation to the Broadview Six prosecution, where a judge criticized grand-jury conduct and charges against six protesters were later dismissed. The firm and individual Democrats were not established as wrongdoing.
description_long: An August 2026 Emptywheel post focused on the role of Assistant U.S. Attorney Matthew Skiba in a Chicago investigation involving Authentic Campaigns, a Democratic political consulting firm once co-owned by Loren Merchan, daughter of New York judge Juan Merchan. The post summarized New York Times reporting that Chicago prosecutors obtained a subpoena for the firm, which had done work for Democratic clients, and identified Skiba and colleague William Hogan as the career prosecutors who secured it. The firm’s connection to Judge Merchan drew attention because he presided over Trump’s New York hush-money trial; the subpoena itself concerned the consulting firm and political communications, not a public finding that the judge had acted improperly. Emptywheel also connected Skiba to the Broadview Six prosecution, a separate case involving six protesters accused of assaulting federal agents during the 2025 Midway Blitz immigration crackdown. That case ended after a judge raised concerns about how prosecutors handled the grand jury. The blog argues the investigation was politically motivated and questions the U.S. attorney’s office’s handling of both matters. Those are the author’s interpretations. The material reviewed establishes the subpoena and the prosecutors’ identities as reported, but does not establish that the investigation was retaliation or that Skiba personally targeted Democrats for an improper purpose. The investigation’s outcome and any legal findings about its purpose are not specified in this account.

corrected_wording.original_claim: Matthew Skiba targeted Democrats in a politicized investigation and sought to intimidate political opponents.
corrected_wording.corrected: A report identifies Skiba as one of two prosecutors who secured a subpoena for a Democratic consulting firm tied to Judge Juan Merchan’s daughter. The claim that this was political retaliation is the source author’s interpretation, not an established finding.

source_access_notes: Opened the supplied Emptywheel commentary. Used a same-event report reproducing the New York Times account for the subpoena context; the original NYT page was inaccessible.
blockers: The reviewed reports do not establish the investigation’s outcome or a finding of political retaliation.
rationale: Changed the categorical accusation into an attributed account of the subpoena and the commentator’s interpretation, while separating the distinct Broadview Six case.
